plain_english: Things themselves don't matter — but how you use them does. So how do you stay calm and steady while still being careful? Not careless, but not stressed out either? Think of people playing dice. The dice don't matter. The counters don't matter. You can't control what numbers come up. But using whatever you roll well and skillfully — that's your job. Life works the same way. Your main task is this: separate things clearly. Say to yourself: 'External things are not up to me. My choices are up to me.' Where should you look for good and bad? Inside yourself, in the things that actually belong to you. But for everything that doesn't belong to you, don't call it good or bad, helpful or harmful, or anything like that.
original_excerpt: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent. How then shall a man preserve firmness and tranquillity, and at the same time be careful and neither rash nor negligent? If he imitates those who play at dice. The counters are indifferent; the dice are indifferent. How do I know what the cast will be? But to use carefully and dexterously the cast of the dice, this is my business. Thus then in life also the chief business is this: distinguish and separate things, and say: Externals are not in my power: will is in my power. Where shall I seek the good and the bad? Within, in the things which are my own. But in what does not belong to you call nothing either good or bad, or profit or damage or anything of the kind.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: So what then? Should we be careless with external things? Absolutely not. Being careless damages your will and goes against your nature. You should act carefully because how you use things matters. But you should also act firmly and calmly because the things themselves don't matter. Here's the key: when something truly doesn't matter, no one can stop you or force you. When someone can stop you or force you, getting that thing isn't up to you — so it's neither good nor bad. But how you use it? That's either good or bad. And that use is up to you. It's hard to combine these two attitudes: being careful like someone who cares about things, while staying firm like someone who doesn't care about them. But it's not impossible. And if it were impossible, happiness would be impossible too.
original_excerpt: What then? Should we use such things carelessly? In no way: for this on the other hand is bad for the faculty of the will, and consequently against nature; but we should act carefully because the use is not indifferent, and we should also act with firmness and freedom from perturbations because the material is indifferent. For where the material is not indifferent, there no man can hinder me or compel me. Where I can be hindered and compelled, the obtaining of those things is not in my power, nor is it good or bad; but the use is either bad or good, and the use is in my power. But it is difficult to mingle and to bring together these two things—the carefulness of him who is affected by the matter (or things about him), and the firmness of him who has no regard for it; but it is not impossible: and if it is, happiness is impossible.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: Think of it like taking a sea voyage. What can you do? You can pick the ship's captain, the crew, when to leave, the right moment to go. Then a storm hits. What else should you worry about? Your part is done. The rest belongs to someone else — the captain. But what if the ship is sinking? What then? You do the only thing you can. You don't drown full of fear. You don't scream or blame God. You know that everything born must die. You're not immortal. You're human, part of the whole — like an hour is part of the day. You show up like the hour does, then pass like the hour does. So what difference does it make how you die? Suffocation or fever — you have to go somehow.
original_excerpt: But we should act as we do in the case of a voyage. What can I do? I can choose the master of the ship, the sailors, the day, the opportunity. Then comes a storm. What more have I to care for? for my part is done. The business belongs to another, the master. But the ship is sinking—what then have I to do? I do the only thing that I can, not to be drowned full of fear, nor screaming nor blaming God, but knowing that what has been produced must also perish: for I am not an immortal being, but a man, a part of the whole, as an hour is a part of the day: I must be present like the hour, and past like the hour. What difference then does it make to me how I pass away, whether by being suffocated or by a fever, for I must pass through some such means.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: How can we say some external things are natural and others unnatural? Think of it this way: imagine we were separated from society. I could tell a foot that it's natural for it to stay clean. But if you think of the foot as part of the whole body, then it makes sense for it to step in mud, walk on thorns, and sometimes even be cut off for the good of the entire body. Otherwise, it's no longer really a foot. We should think about ourselves the same way. What are you? A human being. If you think of yourself as separate from other people, then it seems natural to live to old age, be rich, and stay healthy.
original_excerpt: How then is it said that some external things are according to nature and others contrary to nature? It is said as it might be said if we were separated from union (or society): for to the foot I shall say that it is according to nature for it to be clean; but if you take it as a foot and as a thing not detached (independent), it will befit it both to step into the mud and tread on thorns, and sometimes to be cut off for the good of the whole body; otherwise it is no longer a foot. We should think in some such way about ourselves also. What are you? A man. If you consider yourself as detached from other men, it is according to nature to live to old age, to be rich, to be healthy.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: But if you see yourself as a human being and part of something bigger, then sometimes you need to get sick for the sake of that bigger whole. Sometimes you need to travel and face danger. Sometimes you need to go without. Sometimes you even need to die young. So why does this bother you? Don't you know that a foot is no longer a foot once it's cut off from the body? In the same way, you're no longer human if you're separated from other humans. What is a human being? A part of a community. First, the great community of gods and humans. Then the smaller community right around you, which is like a mini version of that universal community.
original_excerpt: But if you consider yourself as a man and a part of a certain whole, it is for the sake of that whole that at one time you should be sick, at another time take a voyage and run into danger, and at another time be in want, and in some cases die prematurely. Why then are you troubled? Do you not know, that as a foot is no longer a foot if it is detached from the body, so you are no longer a man if you are separated from other men. For what is a man? A part of a state, of that first which consists of gods and of men; then of that which is called next to it, which is a small image of the universal state.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care

plain_english: So what if I have to go to court? What if someone else gets sick, or sails across the ocean, or dies, or gets convicted? Yes, these things will happen. In a world this big, with so many people living together, such things are bound to happen to some people and not others. Your job, since you're here, is to say what you should say and handle these situations properly. Then someone says, "I'm going to accuse you of wronging me." Go ahead — good luck with that. I've done my part. Whether you've done yours is something you need to figure out. There's a real risk you might not even notice if you haven't.
original_excerpt: What then must I be brought to trial; must another have a fever, another sail on the sea, another die, and another be condemned? Yes, for it is impossible in such a universe of things, among so many living together, that such things should not happen, some to one and others to others. It is your duty then since you are come here, to say what you ought, to arrange these things as it is fit. Then some one says, "I shall charge you with doing me wrong." Much good may it do you: I have done my part; but whether you also have done yours, you must look to that; for there is some danger of this too, that it may escape your notice.
source_reference: Discourses, How Magnanimity is Consistent with Care
